World

Police fire teargas as French school protests cause ‘heaviest toll in decades’

Reuters

06 October, 2026 11:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Tilman Blasshofer, Cecile Mantovani and Lucien Libert STRASBOURG/LYON/PARIS, Oct 6 (Reuters) – Police fired tear gas at protesters outside French high schools on Tuesday as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent school protests in decades.

The protests, in which a teenager lost a hand on Monday, were the latest manifestation of public anger in a country where the far right and far left are surging ahead of a presidential election in the spring.

The government is under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, and has struggled with basic tasks such as passing a budget since President Emmanuel Macron’s allies lost their majority in a 2024 parliamentary vote.

Show Full Article

Lecornu told lawmakers at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had so far been injured in clashes, “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system”. His office said more than 700 police officers were also hurt.

Macron has convened Lecornu and other senior ministers at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, broadcaster BFM reported.

In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs reading “The state has killed national education”. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.

In Strasbourg, Lyon, Rennes and Paris, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

The Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.

By late afternoon they said they were still clashing with a small contingent of people. Three storefronts had been damaged.

The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide.

“There is such a gap between the elites and us,” said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.

The High School Students Union said more than half of France’s high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.

Students complain about schools facing basic maintenance problems, from water leaks to rat infestations.

THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS

Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and in some places deteriorated into urban violence.

France’s interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted for unspecified crimes, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said.

A teenager’s hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police grenade intended to be non-lethal.

“They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters,” said Omar Slaouti, a high-school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris. “If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake.”

Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the unrest. LFI denies the accusation.

“All the young people are in the streets. Everywhere there aren’t police, everything is going smoothly,” said Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI’s presidential candidate.

PRIME MINISTER PROMISES A RESPONSE

Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.

The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.

Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government’s words were not enough: “That’s all fine and dandy, but that’s not what’s going to change the daily lives of our children,” she said.

Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.

The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France’s growing debt, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push the cost of borrowing higher. The yield on France’s 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.

The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.

Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring’s election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

French spending on education has lagged inflation and the country’s students are trailing their OECD peers in overall performance, data from the PISA 2025 assessment shows.

item.title: Allemagne-Un ancien directeur du renseignement arrêté pour des soupçons de trahison
item.description: L'ancien chef du service allemand du renseignement extérieur (BND), August Hanning, a été arrêté mardi pour des soupçons de tentative de trahison, une affaire qui constitue l'un des plus importants scandales ayant éclaboussé les services des renseignements allemands depuis la Guerre froide.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'ancien chef du service allemand du renseignement extérieur (BND), August Hanning, a été arrêté mardi pour des soupçons de tentative de trahison, une affaire qui constitue l'un des plus importants scandales ayant éclaboussé les services des renseignements allemands depuis la Guerre froide. August Hanning est accusé par le parquet d'avoir payé pour se procurer des documents secrets après avoir quitté ses fonctions et d'avoir utilisé ces documents pour effectuer une analyse au bénéfice d'un service étranger du renseignement. Les procureurs n'ont pas précisé dans l'immédiat de quel service étranger il s'agissait ni si l'analyse en question a effectivement été transmise à son destinataire voulu. D'après le magazine d'information Der Spiegel, les enquêteurs étudient un possible lien avec l'Azerbaïdjan, alors qu'August Hanning aurait été en contact avec un agent de ce pays. Le parquet fédéral a décliné une demande de commentaire, de même que la chancellerie. Aucun commentaire n'a pu être obtenu auprès d'August Hanning. Jamais, auparavant, un ex-chef du service du renseignement extérieur n'avait été arrêté en Allemagne, dont les relations en matière de renseignements avec des pays alliés pourraient pâtir de cette affaire, a déclaré un élu sécuritaire de haut rang. Dans un communiqué, le parquet a déclaré qu'August Hanning était "fortement suspecté d'espionnage perfide, d'avoir obtenu des secrets d'Etat, de tentative de trahison et d'espionnage". Selon les procureurs, August Hanning était convenu avec le responsable de bureau du BND, cinq ans après son départ du service, dont il a occupé la présidence pendant sept ans jusqu'en 2005, de recevoir des renseignements confidentiels en échange de paiements. Ce responsable de bureau, identifié comme étant Manfred D., dans le respect des règles de confidentialité en Allemagne, a également été arrêté mardi. Les deux hommes devaient comparaître devant un juge de la Cour fédérale de justice. L'AFFAIRE NE CONCERNERAIT PAS LA RUSSIE Manfred D. a été responsable de bureau du BND pour plusieurs présidents successifs du service, jusqu'en mars dernier, ce qui lui a potentiellement permis d'accéder à certains renseignements toujours d'actualité au moment où, d'après les procureurs, des documents ont été "siphonnés" du BND. Quelque 2.000 documents auraient été fournis par Manfred D. au fil des années, ont dit les procureurs, ajoutant que parmi ces documents figuraient des éléments classifiés destinés uniquement à un usage interne au BND et à des compte-rendus auprès de représentants de haut rang à la chancellerie. Selon le journal Sueddeutsche Zeitung, les documents en question concernent le programme nucléaire iranien et l'armée russe, de même que des documents classés secrets transmis par des services de renseignement alliés à propos d'autres pays. Les procureurs accusent August Hanning d'avoir utilisé des informations classifiées transmises par Manfred D. pour préparer une analyse destinée à un officier d'un service étranger du renseignement et d'avoir pendant des années partagé des informations politiques avec un représentant de ce service. Cette affaire ne concerne pas la Russie, selon une information obtenue par le Sueddeutsche Zeitung. L'actuel président du BND a déclaré que le service a lancé une enquête interne approfondie dès que les premiers soupçons sont apparus. "Il ne peut y avoir aucun compromis sur la sécurité interne", a ajouté Martin Jäger.

item.title: Why have India-US trade talks stalled again and what's next?
item.description: Senior officials in India and the United States have indicated long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral trade agreement have stalled, again.
item.dc:creator: Shivangi Acharya, Manoj Kumar
item.content:encoded: Senior officials in India and the United States have indicated long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral trade agreement have stalled, again. Both nations had agreed to a [USN:L1N3YY0U1 TEXT:"framework for the deal"] in February which brought down to 18% [USN:L1N3UJ03Y TEXT:"from 50%"] the punitive tariff on most Indian goods imposed in August last year after a previous round of [USN:L4N3TT0LO TEXT:"talks collapsed"]. In the meantime, the Supreme Court invalidated US President Donald Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to a 10% [USN:L1N3ZG0T5 TEXT:"baseline rate"]. But a final deal between two of the world's biggest economies remains elusive. WHY HAVE TRADE TALKS HIT A WALL? Trade talks have [USN:L1N45R03N TEXT:"reached a "plateau""] with little room for manoeuvre, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this week, following United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer's comment that a deal is [USN:S0N40K049 TEXT:"not "imminent"]." Neither side has detailed reasons for the delay in finalising the deal. But talks in the past months have met with complications, most recently [USN:L1N4590XN TEXT:"a new US law"] that paves the way for up to 100% tariffs on Indian goods because of New Delhi's purchase of Russian oil. Those purchases have not been significantly reduced. The potentially stiff levy goes against New Delhi's [USN:L4N42U08S TEXT:"efforts to secure"] tariff terms better than peer economies, including Vietnam and China. A deal has also been held back because Washington is [USN:L1N4290B6 TEXT:"yet to complete"] a Section 301 trade investigation on several nations over alleged excess industrial capacity. The probe is to evaluate whether such overproduction is hurting or undercutting American industries. Unless this probe is completed, it is hard to tell what final tariff Indian goods will attract. Overall, bilateral ties between India and the US have been rocky this past year, casting a shadow on [USN:L1N45904J TEXT:"efforts to stabilise"] their trade partnership. Events including a [USN:L1N42K089 TEXT:"US military attack"] on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers and [USN:L1N3TP08X TEXT:"India rejecting"] Trump's repeated claim of brokering a ceasefire with Pakistan have hurt relations. WHAT IS AT STAKE? The US is India's largest export market and exports have so far been [USN:L4N3XL16E TEXT:"resilient"]. India's goods exports to the United States rose to $42.79 billion in April-August from $40.39 billion a year earlier. In the fiscal year 2025/26, India enjoyed a nearly $34 billion trade surplus with the US. India says many of its largest export categories to the US, including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, are not subject to the current 10% levy. But analysts say that in the absence of a trade deal, India risks higher US tariffs from the ongoing trade probe and purchase of Russian oil, even if it could negotiate for waivers under the sanctions law. Another increase in tariffs could hurt businesses, dent market sentiment and hurt the Indian currency, which is already trading close to record lows. WHAT MORE DO THE TWO SIDES WANT? India is striving to protect politically sensitive sectors, particularly agriculture, while securing [USN:L1N43F08Q TEXT:"better tariff treatment"] for its exporters. India has sought to keep dairy, poultry, rice, wheat and other farm products outside the scope of market-opening commitments. It wants greater certainty over US tariffs before making concessions. The Trump administration wants India to cut Russian oil purchases, arguing Indian purchases of Russian crude help finance the war in Ukraine. India says decisions on where to source fuel are driven by [USN:L4N45A0SX TEXT:"the energy needs"] of its 1.4-billion-strong population. Russian crude became particularly important after Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine because it was available at discounted prices. The war in the Middle East and resulting disruptions have sharpened the calculation over energy imports. ARE FURTHER TALKS PLANNED? US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to visit India later this month, when two-way talks could make some progress. Modi and Trump, who spoke by phone on September 30, are also expected to speak again soon to review progress. Modi is expected to visit the US in December for a G20 leaders' meet.

item.title: Planned Moldova-Romania power line to be named after Trump
item.description: A planned high-voltage power line linking Romania and Moldova will be named the "Trump Liberty Line," the US embassy in Chisinau said on Monday, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of US President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A planned high-voltage power line linking Romania and Moldova will be named the "Trump Liberty Line," the US embassy in Chisinau said on Monday, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of US President Donald Trump. The embassy said in a post on X that the project, "backed by a $130 million US government investment", would strengthen Moldova's energy security and independence "The Government of the Republic of Moldova supports initiatives that benefit the citizens of the Republic of Moldova, especially those that ensure the country's security and energy infrastructure," government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici told Reuters "The Romanian government has always supported interconnecting projects between Romania and Moldova, and the fact the United States supports and finances them only reconfirms their strategic importance," said government spokeswoman Ioana Dogioiu. Moldova, one of Europe's poorest countries and a candidate for European Union membership, imports most of its electricity via existing links with Romania and Ukraine. Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure have disrupted those supplies in the past Trump's name has been attached to a growing number of projects around the world, including a proposed transport corridor through Armenia and a planned military base in Poland, as governments seek to win favour with the US president

item.title: For Trump’s Treasury, the sting is in the auction ‘tail’
item.description: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news. The Treasury plans to sell nearly $120 billion of debt this week, the first sales outside of T-bills in two weeks: $58 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $39 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday, and $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. These might normally be non-events, but they're under increasing scrutiny because the September 22-24 auctions were remarkably weak, particularly the five-year note auction on Sept. 23, which helped spark the biggest rise in bond yields since April last year. Yields have not come down since and have instead powered ahead to multi-decade highs across most maturities. It's worth stating that there's next to zero chance that the US would ever have a "failed" debt auction. Primary dealers – the 26 Wall Street banks and institutions currently approved by the New York Fed as Treasury market makers – will always participate. They effectively underwrite the sales, ensuring the $30 trillion US debt market – the most liquid market in the world – functions smoothly. This, in turn, keeps the entire global financial system chugging along, as well. Trillions of dollars of global debt, assets, and market derivatives use Treasuries as a reference. US government bonds are also the collateral used to lubricate the pipes of US and global financial plumbing - repo agreements, interbank lending, and funding. In short, as long as US debt is the lynchpin of the global financial system, there will always be buyers at Treasury auctions. The issue, as ever, is the price at which these sales clear. Right now, borrowing costs on the secondary market are the highest since the mid to early 2000s, so it is reasonable to assume that Treasury will pay comparably high rates on the primary market. But as the most recent auctions have shown, there is also still room for negative surprises. TOO BIG TO TAIL? The $70 billion sale of five-year notes on September 23 was one of the most alarming in recent memory. Demand as measured by the 'bid-to-cover' ratio was the lowest in nine years. Treasury ultimately sold the notes at 5.033%, which was more than three basis points above the market yield at the bidding deadline. Three basis points might not sound like a lot, but for a five-year auction, that’s extraordinary. It was the largest so-called "tail" since June 2022. To find the last time a five-year auction had a 3 bps "tail," JP Morgan analysts note, you have to go all the way back to 2011, when a brewing debt ceiling crisis would lead to a credit rating downgrade that August. Moving back to the present, concerns about the dire US fiscal outlook have pushed up long-term borrowing costs. As a result, the Trump administration is widely expected to gradually shift the weight of the Treasury’s huge borrowing requirements towards the shorter - and cheaper - end of the curve. This is why the five-year auction two weeks ago caused such alarm. "Tails" of 3 bps are common in longer bond auctions, but not in sales of debt that sit right in the so-called "belly" of the yield curve. If Treasury is being forced to pay higher premiums to shift these notes, then Houston, we have a problem. Fat auction “tails” can be a result of multiple forces, including market volatility on the day itself or more worrying fundamental issues that might erode demand over time. It's often difficult to untangle the two dynamics, as they are not mutually exclusive. On a more optimistic note, these jitters haven’t migrated to the front end of the curve. Yet. Three-year and 10-year yields are up around 50 basis points from their last auctions a month ago, hovering around 4.96% and 5.32%, respectively. The 30-year yield is up around 35 bps at 5.65%. That should be high enough to attract solid demand and ensure smooth sales, right? Probably. But if there’s a sting in the tails, volatility and uncertainty could bite across the market. Investors will be watching like, well, hawks. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X. And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

FAST

The United States has discussed starting reciprocal visits to nuclear sites with China, and plans to continue pushing in meetings in the coming months, CNN reported on Tuesday (Oct 6), citing sources familiar with the matter.

The idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by China in meetings with US officials this year and visits to US Department of Energy national laboratories and equivalent Chinese facilities were discussed, CNN said, citing a source.

The discussions between US and Chinese officials have mainly been on the sidelines of gatherings by the UN Security Council's five veto-wielding permanent members, CNN reported.

Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The White House and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment outside business hours.

US President Donald Trump called for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, China and Russia when he met President Xi Jinping last month. However, the two leaders did not discuss the possibility of nuclear site visits during their talks, the CNN report said, citing a US official.

Beijing has said its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of Russia and the US, something it says makes its participation in such talks unnecessary.

Another meeting between Trump and Xi is widely considered likely this year, potentially at November's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China or during Group of 20 meetings in the US in December.

By the time the two leaders meet again, it is expected that further lower-level discussions on possible nuclear site visits will have taken place, CNN said.

item.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
item.description: STOCKHOLM: The Belgian-American Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work creating an Antarctic observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that can reveal otherwise inaccessible information about the cosmos.Halzen, 82, realised that pristine ice at th
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:

Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt

Eva Olsson, Ellen Moons, and Mark Pearce sit as they announce Francis Halzen as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics during a press conference at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct 6, 2026. (Photo: TT News Agency/Christine Olsson via REUTERS)

FAST

STOCKHOLM: The Belgian-American Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work creating an Antarctic observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that can reveal otherwise inaccessible information about the cosmos. Halzen, 82, realised that pristine ice at the South Pole could be used to track such neutrinos, sometimes known as "ghost particles" for the way they pass through the Earth without a trace, only interacting with matter extremely rarely. "The messengers bring information from the cosmos," Eva Olsson, of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a press conference. "They open the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars." HALZEN HAILED FOR DETECTING "MESSENGERS FROM THE COSMOS" The interactions registered by the IceCube observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said.

In 2014, the US-based Smithsonian magazine dubbed Halzen "Neutrino Man" when giving him one of its Ingenuity Awards, acclaiming him for an "amazing experiment (that) heralds the beginning of a new era in astronomy". It even published a comic illustrating his life: "How One Physicist’s Pursuit of the Cosmos Took Off in Antarctica". The observatory - in effect a telescope that shows neutrinos instead of light - is set in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, which extends to a depth of 2,500 metres below the surface near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. More than 5,000 sensors await blips from the nearly massless high-energy neutrinos, which unlike other particles do not lose energy or change direction, in the hope of tracing their paths back to exploding stars, gamma-ray bursts, and cataclysmic phenomena involving black holes and neutron stars. They can expect to register about one per day. Halzen, a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States, first presented his idea in 1988 for capturing neutrino traces at the South Pole, but the project was not completed until 2011. "I have to emphasise how lucky I was because, when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself," Halzen told the press conference by telephone. Neutrinos are electrically neutral, undisturbed by any magnetic field, which means that, in contrast to electromagnetic waves such as visible light, the direction from which they arrive points directly back to their source.

Related:

Medicine Nobel goes to US-German trio for pioneering light-based control of cells

FRUITS OF HALZEN'S RESEARCH YET TO COME The observatory has determined that high-energy neutrinos originate within but also far outside our own Milky Way galaxy, setting in motion an interstellar quest to find the objects and processes that create them. Through the long winter at the South Pole, when bringing anything in or out is difficult as temperatures below minus 50°C (minus 58 Fahrenheit) preclude even aircraft landing, a skeleton crew of "winterovers" has to maintain the observatory. The station, home to many other activities, can house as many as 150 people and has an industrial kitchen, dining room, gym and even a greenhouse. Last week it celebrated the sun's return above the horizon after six months of night with a six-hole ice-golf tournament. An extension, IceCube-Gen2, encompassing 8 cubic kilometres of ice, is planned to become operational in 2033 and will be able to detect 10 times as many neutrinos, including much weaker ones. Halzen said the main fruits of his work were yet to be seen and that it was too early to say exactly what it could reveal about the universe. "The real excitement is that I cannot answer that question yet," he said. "This is just an introduction to the science, the astronomy is still to come." WINNERS FROM EINSTEIN TO BOHR AND THE CURIES Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever congratulated Halzen on the recognition of "a life dedicated to unraveling the greatest secrets of the cosmos through its most minuscule manifestations". The physics laureate receives an award of 12 million Swedish crowns (US$1.2 million). Past winners include several other neutrino research pioneers, for instance Japan's Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald from Canada in 2015. The Nobel Prizes were established under the will of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was built in part on the invention of dynamite. Physics was prominent in Nobel's will and the prize remains one of the discipline's highest distinctions. Over the decades, it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe. Among past laureates are some of the most celebrated figures in science, including Albert Einstein, Marie and Pierre Curie, Max Planck and Niels Bohr, whose work helped establish the foundations of modern physics. The prize is presented in Stockholm on Dec 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.

Source: Reuters/fh

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe Les valeurs à suivre mercredi à la Bourse de Paris et en Europe : ANALYSE: L'euro fait les frais des turbulences sur la dette souveraine française LONDRES, 6 octobre (Reuters) - La dépréciation de l'euro constitue le dernier signal d'alarme pour les responsables de la zone euro, qui constatent que la hausse vertigineuse des coûts de financement de la France, plongée dans un débat budgétaire périlleux, commence à se répercuter sur l'ensemble du bloc. Paramount a finalisé le rachat de Warner Bros pour créer Skydance 6 octobre (Reuters) - Paramount Skydance a finalisé mardi son rachat de Warner Bros Discovery pour 110 milliards de dollars (97,80 milliards d'euros), donnant ainsi naissance à Skydance et confiant à son directeur général David Ellison, les rênes de l'une des plus grandes entreprises mondiales du divertissement. Le français BPCE acquiert une participation de 7% dans la banque espagnole Sabadell MADRID, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le groupe bancaire français BPCE a acquis une participation d'environ 7% dans la banque espagnole Sabadell par le biais d'achats sur le marché et d'instruments financiers, avec l'intention de devenir un actionnaire à long terme, ont annoncé mardi les deux établissements. Carine Damois nouvelle directrice financière de Renault, Duncan Minto s'en va Renault Group a annoncé lundi la nomination au poste de directrice financière de Carine Damois, qui succède à Duncan Minto à un moment charnière pour le groupe au losange. Schneider Electric chute en Bourse après l'annonce du rachat de PTC pour €20,2 mds Schneider Electric chutait de quelque 9% lundi en milieu de matinée à la Bourse de Paris, après l'annonce de l'acquisition de 100% du capital du spécialiste des logiciels industriels américain PTC sur la base d'une valorisation à 22,6 milliards de dollars (20,2 milliards d'euros). Les marchés brésiliens attendus en hausse après la percée de Flávio Bolsonaro Les marchés brésiliens devraient rebondir lundi après la performance surprise de Flávio Bolsonaro au premier tour de la présidentielle dimanche, selon des analystes interrogés par Reuters. Le sénateur de droite a recueilli 47% des voix, contre environ 45% pour le président sortant Lula, que les sondages donnaient en tête avec trois points d’avance. L'ascension de Revolut, devenue une rivale des grandes banques européennes, valorisée €103 mds La fintech britannique Revolut s'est hissée au rang de start-up la plus valorisée d'Europe, posant un défi pour les grandes banques classique au vu de sa croissance fulgurante en un peu plus de 10 années d'existence. La reconstitution des stocks de brut et de carburant pourrait prendre deux ans, selon le PDG d'Aramco La pénurie de pétrole brut et de carburants raffinés devrait s'aggraver, et la reconstitution des stocks mondiaux, puisés à titre de mesure d'urgence, pourrait prendre deux ans, a déclaré lundi Amin Nasser, directeur général de Saudi Aramco , lors de la conférence Energy Intelligence à Londres. La Première ministre s'engage à respecter une discipline budgétaire La Première ministre japonaise Sanae Takaichi, s'est engagée lundi à "maîtriser" les émissions obligataires et à agir rapidement face aux turbulences du marché, cherchant ainsi à rassurer les investisseurs inquiets de la détérioration des finances publiques du pays.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: L'Iran doit réduire ses activités d'enrichissement d'uranium pour mettre fin à la guerre, dit Vance
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Iran doit réduire ses activités d'enrichissement d'uranium pour mettre fin à la guerre, dit Vance FAIRBANKS, Alaska, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le vice-président américain J.D. Vance a déclaré dans une interview accordée à Reuters que l'Iran réduire de manière "significative" sa capacité d'enrichissement nucléaire pour satisfaire aux exigences des Etats-Unis et mettre fin à la guerre. Des marins disparus en mer Noire après une frappe de drone sur leur navire au large de la Bulgarie BELGRADE, 6 octobre (Reuters) - L'équipage d'un navire marchand est porté disparu après que leur bateau a coulé à la suite d'une attaque de drone subie pendant qu'il naviguait dans la zone économique bulgare de la mer Noire, a déclaré le Premier ministre bulgare, Rouman Radev, qualifiant l'incident de violation flagrante du droit international. Ukraine: La Russie lance des attaques contre Kyiv, deux morts 7 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a mené tôt mercredi des frappes contre Kyiv, faisant deux morts et endommageant des bâtiments et des entrepôts, ont déclaré les autorités locales. Yémen: L'aéroport d'Aden visé par des missiles houthis 7 octobre (Reuters) - Les Houthis yéménites, proches de l'Iran, ont attaqué mercredi l'aéroport international d'Aden à l'aide de missiles balistiques et de drones chargés d'explosifs, a dit le ministère yéménite des Transports, nouveau signe de l'intensification des combats. Kosovo: Le Parlement élit un nouveau président, évite des élections anticipées PRISTINA, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Le Parlement du Kosovo a élu l'économiste Justina Shiroka Pula à la présidence du pays, une fonction essentiellement honorifique, juste avant l'expiration du délai prévu par la Constitution, évitant ainsi de nouvelles élections anticipées. Allemagne: Un ancien directeur du renseignement arrêté pour des soupçons de trahison BERLIN, 6 octobre (Reuters) - L'ancien chef du service allemand du renseignement extérieur (BND), August Hanning, a été arrêté mardi pour des soupçons de tentative de trahison, une affaire qui constitue l'un des plus importants scandales ayant éclaboussé les services des renseignements allemands depuis la Guerre froide. Deux Palestiniens tués par des frappes israéliennes selon les secours LE CAIRE, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Des frappes israéliennes ont tué au moins deux Palestiniens dans la bande de Gaza mardi, selon les autorités sanitaires locales. L'AfD peine à former son premier gouvernement régional après sa victoire en Saxe-Anhalt MAGDEBOURG, Allemagne, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le parti d'extrême droite "Alternative pour l'Allemagne" (AfD) s'est réuni mardi à l'occasion de la première séance du Parlement régional de Saxe-Anhalt, mais un mois après le choc de sa victoire électorale dans ce Land, le parti n'est pas encore en mesure de former un gouvernement régional. Royaume-Uni: Trois Iraniens jugés pour espionnage à l'encontre de journalistes LONDRES, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Trois hommes iraniens sont accusés d'avoir espionné des journalistes au Royaume-Uni pour le compte des services de renseignement de Téhéran, ont déclaré mardi les procureurs devant un jury londonien. Le Kremlin met en garde la Lituanie sur sa décision de lever l'interdiction des armes nucléaires MOSCOU, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le Kremlin a averti mardi que la décision, qui doit encore être confirmée, prise par Lituanie de lever l'interdiction constitutionnelle d'accueillir des armes nucléaires sur son territoire pourrait entraîner une nouvelle escalade dans la région.

item.title: OFRSP Summary
item.description: Football: Messi fait ses adieux à l'équipe d'Argentine
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Football: Messi fait ses adieux à l'équipe d'Argentine BUENOS AIRES, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Lionel Messi a donné mardi une dernière leçon de maître sous le maillot bleu et blanc, le capitaine de l'équipe de football d'Argentine ayant mis un point d'orgue à sa carrière internationale de 21 ans en marquant un but lors d'un match amical contre le Bénin. Basket: Les actionnaires de l'Euroligue rejettent l'offre de la NBA, les négociations restent ouvertes CERNOBBIO, Italie 6 octobre (Reuters) - Les clubs actionnaires de l'Euroligue de basket (C1) ont rejeté mardi une offre de la NBA pour un partenariat entre les deux entités alors que la toute puissante ligue nord-américaine a prévu de lancer une ligue européenne en 2027. Football: La Fédération norvégienne saisit deux commissions de la Fifa sur la gouvernance et l'éthique STOCKHOLM, 6 octobre (Reuters) - La Fédération norvégienne de football (NFF) a annoncé mardi avoir déposé deux requêtes parallèles auprès de deux commissions de la Fifa concernant trois récents dossiers qui ont suscité la controverse dans le football mondial. Sept pays, dont l'Inde, candidats pour organiser les Jeux olympiques de 2036 BERLIN, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Sept pays, dont l'Inde, l'Allemagne et le Qatar, sont en lice pour accueillir les Jeux olympiques d'été de 2036, a annoncé mardi le Comité international olympique (CIO). Football: Trois victoires et des promesses pour les débuts de Zidane à la tête des Bleus PARIS, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Zinédine Zidane a conclu son premier rassemblement en tant que sélectionneur de l'équipe de France invaincu en Ligue des nations et avec quelques promesses, alors que ses débuts étaient particulièrement attendus après 14 ans sous les ordres de Didier Deschamps. Tennis: Blessé au genou, Sinner met fin à sa saison 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le numéro un mondial de tennis Jannik Sinner a annoncé mardi que sa saison 2026 était d'ores et déjà terminée en raison d'une blessure à un genou nécessitant un traitement. Football-Les Bleus renversent la Belgique grâce à leurs remplaçants L'équipe de France a renversé la Belgique (4-1), lundi soir au Stade de France, grâce à quatre buts inscrits dans le dernier quart d'heure, tous par des remplaçants, pour s'offrir un succès précieux et conserver la tête du groupe A1 de la Ligue des nations. Football: Accusé d'infractions financières, Manchester City fait appel Manchester City a annoncé vendredi faire appel du jugement d'une commission indépendante qui a reconnu le club coupable de graves infractions aux règles financières de la Premier League entre 2009 et 2018. Football-Les Bleus accrochés par l'Italie pour la première de Zidane au Stade de France L'équipe de France a concédé le nul vendredi face à l'Italie (1-1) lors de la troisième journée de la phase de groupes de la Ligue des nations, le premier petit accroc de l'ère Zinédine Zidane, qui dirigeait son premier match au Stade de France en tant que sélectionneur. Football: L'Union des associations arabes de football exprime son soutien à Infantino L'Union des associations arabes de football (UAFA) a exprimé son soutien au président de la Fifa, Gianni Infantino, à l'issue d'une réunion de son conseil d'administration qui s'est tenue jeudi à Djeddah.
